newsitem.title: CANADA: Hong Kong's Lee asks Canada, U.S. to defend rights.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Lee asks Canada, U.S. to defend rights.

text.p: Leaders of Hong Kong's Democratic Party on Thursday urged the United States and Canada to stand up for civil rights in the territory as China takes over later this year.

Party leader Martin Lee told a news conference in Vancouver that the two governments should not shrink from speaking out because of concerns about the potential impact on their trade relations with China.
Lee said he wants to convey this message to U.S. President Bill Clinton and Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien during a month-long trip to North America that began on Wednesday.
Neither Ottawa nor Washington has yet responded to his requests for meetings with the two leaders, he said.

"I want to explain to them, although I understand how important China trade must be to both to Canada and the USA, there is no reason for them to sacrifice Hong Kong's freedoms in order to have more China trade," Lee told reporters.
"China trade and Hong Kong's freedoms are not mutually exclusive," he said.
Hong Kong, a British colony for 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule on July 1 and the Democratic Party has fought against Chinese plans to curb democracy and civil rights laws in the territory.
Lee, anti-communist activist Szeto Wah and legislator Andrew Cheng are touring the United States and Canada to raise money and awareness for their cause.
The United States is seeking to improve tense relations with China, and Hong Kong is expected to come up when U.S. Vice President Al Gore visits Beijing next week.
Canada has emphasised its growing trade with China and Ottawa has favoured a diplomatic approach over human rights issues that seeks to avoid angering Beijing.
Lee praised Canada's announcement on Wednesday that it will continue to waive visa requirements for Hong Kong passport holders after China takes over.

"That is a very good morale booster....I only hope more countries will follow suit," Lee said. So far only Canada, Britain and Singapore have pledged visa-free entry. He plans to lobby the United States for visa-free access as well.
